description: Determine your Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement before entering any negotiation. Your BATNA sets your walk-away point. A negotiator without a BATNA accepts bad deals because walking away feels worse than any offer on the table. Strengthen your BATNA before negotiating.

steps.description: Generate every alternative you have if this negotiation fails. Be specific: what exactly will you do?

inputs.name: negotiation-context
inputs.desc: What you are negotiating for and with whom

inputs.name: what-you-need
inputs.desc: The underlying need the negotiation serves (not just the position)

outputs.name: alternatives-list
outputs.desc: Every realistic alternative if this negotiation produces no agreement, with the specific actions and outcomes for each

outputs.name: alternative-costs
outputs.desc: The cost (time, money, effort, opportunity) of each alternative

process: List every alternative: other suppliers, other buyers, other employers, other candidates, self-provision, delay, or doing nothing. Include alternatives that require effort to create.
Be honest about each alternative: is it real or hypothetical? Can you execute it tomorrow, or does it require months of preparation?
Estimate the value of each alternative: what outcome does it produce, and at what cost?
Include the status quo: what happens if you negotiate nothing and do nothing differently? The status quo is always an alternative.

steps.description: Evaluate alternatives and identify the best one. This is your BATNA. It sets your reservation price.

outputs.name: batna
outputs.desc: The best alternative: the specific action you will take if negotiation fails, with its expected outcome

outputs.name: reservation-price
outputs.desc: The worst deal you should accept: any deal must be better than the BATNA, or you walk away

process: Rank alternatives by net value: outcome minus cost. The highest net value alternative is your BATNA.
Set the reservation price: the deal terms that make you indifferent between the deal and the BATNA. Any deal worse than this, you walk away.
Test the reservation price: would you genuinely walk away at this point? If not, you have overestimated your BATNA.
Write down the BATNA and reservation price before entering the negotiation. Negotiation pressure will tempt you to accept worse deals unless the walk-away point is pre-committed.

steps.description: Strengthen your BATNA before negotiating. A stronger BATNA gives you more power at the table.

outputs.name: strengthening-actions
outputs.desc: Specific actions to improve your BATNA before the negotiation: create new alternatives, improve existing ones, or reduce the cost of exercising them

outputs.name: updated-batna
outputs.desc: The BATNA after strengthening, with the new reservation price

process: Create new alternatives: can you bring additional options into existence before the negotiation? Get another job offer. Find another supplier. Develop an internal capability.
Improve existing alternatives: can you make your best alternative more attractive? Negotiate better terms with the backup option. Reduce the switching cost.
Reduce the cost of exercising the BATNA: can you make walking away cheaper or easier?
Every improvement to the BATNA raises your reservation price and gives you more negotiating power.

description: Map the Zone of Possible Agreement (ZOPA): the range between your reservation price and the other party's reservation price. If the zones overlap, a deal is possible. If they do not overlap, no deal should be made. Understanding the ZOPA prevents wasting time on impossible deals and reveals value on possible ones.

steps.description: Set your reservation price based on your BATNA analysis.

inputs.name: batna
inputs.desc: Your best alternative to a negotiated agreement

inputs.name: negotiation-issues
inputs.desc: All the issues on the table (price, terms, timing, scope)

outputs.name: own-reservation-price
outputs.desc: The worst terms you should accept on each issue

outputs.name: own-target
outputs.desc: The best realistic outcome you aim for on each issue

process: For each issue, set the reservation price: the point at which you are indifferent between this deal and your BATNA.
Set your target: the best outcome you can realistically justify. Research comparable deals, market rates, or precedents to support the target.
The reservation price is private. The target is what you argue for. Never reveal the reservation price.
For multi-issue negotiations: set reservation prices on each issue independently, but consider trade-offs across issues.

steps.description: Estimate the other party's reservation price. You will not know it exactly, but you can estimate it by understanding their alternatives.

inputs.name: counterpart-context
inputs.desc: What you know about the other party's situation, needs, and alternatives

outputs.name: estimated-counterpart-reservation
outputs.desc: Your best estimate of their worst acceptable terms on each issue, with the reasoning

outputs.name: counterpart-batna-estimate
outputs.desc: What you believe their best alternative is, and therefore their walk-away point

process: Research their alternatives: who else can they negotiate with? What happens if they make no deal? What are their costs of delay or switching?
Estimate their reservation price: given their alternatives, what is the worst deal they would still accept?

Look for signals: urgency (they need a deal quickly = lower reservation price), competition (they have many alternatives = higher reservation price), anchoring (their first offer signals where they think the zone is).
This estimate is uncertain. Update it as the negotiation reveals new information.

steps.description: Assess whether a ZOPA exists. If your reservation price is better than their estimated reservation price (from their perspective), there is overlap and a deal is possible.

inputs.name: estimated-counterpart-reservation
inputs.desc: Their estimated reservation prices by issue

outputs.name: zopa-assessment
outputs.desc: Whether a ZOPA exists, its estimated size on each issue, and where the value lies

outputs.name: negotiation-strategy
outputs.desc: If ZOPA exists: aim for deals closer to their reservation price. If no ZOPA: change the deal structure or walk away.

process: Compare the two reservation prices on each issue. If your worst acceptable price is lower than their worst acceptable price (for a seller; reversed for buyer), a ZOPA exists on that issue.
Estimate the ZOPA size: the distance between the two reservation prices. Larger ZOPA means more room to negotiate.
If no ZOPA exists on the primary issue: can you change the deal structure to create one? Add issues, change timing, bundle or unbundle.
If no ZOPA exists and the structure cannot change: walk away. No amount of negotiation skill creates a deal where none is possible.

description: Negotiate based on interests, not positions. Positions are what people say they want. Interests are why they want it. Two people who want the same orange (position conflict) may have different interests: one wants the juice, the other wants the rind. Interest-based negotiation finds deals that positions hide.

steps.description: Uncover the interests behind both parties' positions. Ask why, not what.

inputs.name: negotiation-positions
inputs.desc: What each party says they want

outputs.name: own-interests
outputs.desc: Your underlying interests ranked by importance: substantive (money, terms), procedural (how the process works), relational (the ongoing relationship)

outputs.name: counterpart-interests
outputs.desc: Their likely underlying interests, estimated from their behavior, statements, and situation

process: For your own position on each issue, ask: why do I want this? What underlying need does it serve? What would happen if I got a different position that served the same need?
For their position, ask: why might they want this? What need does it serve for them? If you are not sure, ask them directly: 'Help me understand why this is important to you.'
Rank your interests by importance. Some are essential (deal-breakers), some are important (strong preference), some are nice-to-have (willing to trade).
Look for differences in interest rankings: issues that are high-priority for you but low-priority for them (and vice versa) are where trades create mutual value.

steps.description: Create value by trading across interests. Give on issues that matter less to you; get on issues that matter more.

outputs.name: trade-opportunities
outputs.desc: Pairs of issues where you and they have different priorities, creating room for mutually beneficial trades

outputs.name: value-creating-proposals
outputs.desc: Specific deal proposals that give each party more of what they value most

process: Identify asymmetric valuations: issues where you care a lot and they care little, and vice versa. These are the trade opportunities.
Construct package proposals: 'I will give you X (which you value highly but costs me little) in exchange for Y (which I value highly but costs you little).'
Never negotiate issue by issue. Issue-by-issue negotiation is zero-sum. Package deals allow value creation.

Test proposals with 'What if...' questions: 'What if we extended the timeline but reduced the price?' 'What if we included support but changed the payment terms?' These reveal interest priorities without committing.

steps.description: Resolve remaining disagreements using objective criteria: market rates, precedent, expert opinion, or fair standards. Objective criteria prevent negotiation from becoming a contest of will.

inputs.name: negotiation-context
inputs.desc: The context for finding relevant criteria

outputs.name: applicable-criteria
outputs.desc: For each unresolved issue: the objective criteria that apply (market rate, comparable transaction, industry standard, legal precedent, expert valuation)

outputs.name: criteria-based-resolution
outputs.desc: The resolution suggested by each criterion, with the recommended final terms

process: For each unresolved issue, research objective criteria: what do others pay or receive in comparable situations? What does industry data show? What do experts recommend?
Present criteria, not positions: 'The market rate for this service is X' is stronger than 'I want X.' Criteria depersonalize the disagreement.
If multiple criteria conflict, discuss which is most relevant. Do not cherry-pick the criterion that favors you.
If no objective criteria exist, propose a fair procedure for resolving the issue: split the difference, flip a coin, use an arbitrator, or take turns choosing.

description: Set the anchor: the first number or proposal in a negotiation. Research shows the first offer strongly influences the final outcome. Anchor aggressively but justifiably. An anchor without justification is dismissed. An anchor with a plausible story moves the entire negotiation range.

steps.description: Research the range of reasonable outcomes to determine where to anchor. The anchor must be extreme enough to pull the negotiation your way but plausible enough to be taken seriously.

outputs.name: market-range
outputs.desc: The range of comparable outcomes from research: low end, median, high end, with sources

outputs.name: anchor-position
outputs.desc: The recommended first offer: aggressive but within the range of justifiable positions

process: Research comparable transactions or outcomes: salary data, property comparables, contract terms, industry rates. Collect at least 3-5 data points.
Identify the range: what is the lowest and highest comparable outcome?
Set the anchor at the aggressive end of the justifiable range. For sellers: near the high end. For buyers: near the low end.
The anchor should be beyond your target but within the range of outcomes you can justify with data. An anchor outside the justifiable range will be dismissed and damage credibility.

steps.description: Build the justification for the anchor. The anchor's power comes from the story that accompanies it, not the number alone.

outputs.name: anchor-justification
outputs.desc: The data and reasoning that support the anchor position: comparable transactions, unique value, market conditions, timing factors

outputs.name: anchor-delivery-script
outputs.desc: How to present the anchor: the opening statement that frames the number with its justification

process: Select the 2-3 strongest data points that support the anchor. Quality of evidence matters more than quantity.
Build the narrative: explain why the anchor is the right starting point given the specific circumstances. Reference comparables that favor your position.
Prepare the delivery: state the anchor confidently and immediately provide the justification. 'Based on [data], [comparable], and [factor], I am proposing [anchor].'
Anticipate the counter-anchor: what will they say? Prepare responses to their likely objections.

steps.description: Handle the other party's counter-anchor. Do not let their anchor re-set your expectations. Re-anchor with your own justification.

outputs.name: counter-anchor-response-plan
outputs.desc: How to respond if they anchor first: acknowledge, re-frame, and re-anchor with your own justification

outputs.name: concession-plan
outputs.desc: How to make concessions from the anchor: each concession is smaller than the last and comes with a reason

process: If they anchor first: do not counter immediately. Ask how they arrived at their number. This buys time and may reveal weaknesses in their justification.
Re-anchor: present your own anchor with justification. Do not treat their anchor as a starting point. Treat it as their opening position and present yours.
Make concessions strategically: each concession should be smaller than the previous one (signaling you are approaching your limit) and should come with a reason ('I can move to X because of Y').
Never concede without getting something in return. Unreciprocated concessions signal weakness and invite further demands.

description: Negotiate contracts: identify the terms that matter, understand the standard vs. non-standard terms, negotiate the high-impact terms, and accept the rest. Most contracts are 80% standard and 20% negotiable. Focus on the 20% that determines whether this is a good or bad deal.

steps.description: Classify every contract term as standard (accept), high-impact (negotiate), or deal-breaker (must change or walk away).

inputs.name: deal-priorities
inputs.desc: What matters most in this deal: price, liability, timeline, exclusivity, termination, IP, indemnification

outputs.name: term-classification
outputs.desc: Each term classified: standard (accept as-is), high-impact (worth negotiating), or deal-breaker (non-negotiable requirement)

outputs.name: negotiation-focus-list
outputs.desc: The 3-7 terms worth negotiating, ranked by impact

process: Read every term. For each, ask: if this term were different, would it meaningfully change the value or risk of this deal?
Standard terms: boilerplate language, governing law, notice provisions, standard warranty. Accept these unless they contain unusual provisions.
High-impact terms: pricing, payment terms, termination clauses, liability caps, indemnification, exclusivity, IP ownership, non-compete, auto-renewal. These are where value is created or destroyed.
Deal-breakers: terms you cannot accept under any circumstances. These are non-negotiable. If the other party insists, you walk away.

steps.description: Negotiate the high-impact terms. For each term, know the market standard, your preferred position, and your walk-away.

outputs.name: term-positions
outputs.desc: For each high-impact term: the market standard, your preferred position, your reservation position, and the justification for your preferred position

outputs.name: negotiation-sequence
outputs.desc: The order to negotiate terms: start with terms where agreement is easiest to build momentum

process: For each high-impact term, research the market standard: what do comparable contracts include? This is your baseline.
Set your preferred position: what would make this term most valuable to you? Set your reservation position: the worst acceptable version of this term.
Prepare the justification: why is your preferred position reasonable? Reference market data, comparable deals, or risk analysis.
Negotiate easier terms first. Agreement builds momentum and relationship. Save the hardest terms for after you have established a collaborative dynamic.

steps.description: Scan for hidden risks: terms that seem standard but create outsized exposure. The worst contract terms are the ones that look boring.

inputs.name: contract-terms
inputs.desc: The full contract including negotiated terms

outputs.name: hidden-risk-list
outputs.desc: Terms that create disproportionate risk: unlimited liability, broad indemnification, unilateral amendment, automatic renewal with price increase, assignment without consent

outputs.name: risk-mitigation-requests
outputs.desc: Specific changes to mitigate each hidden risk, with the rationale

process: Scan for unlimited liability: is there a cap? If not, request one. Standard cap: 12 months of fees or the contract value.
Scan for broad indemnification: are you indemnifying them for their own negligence? Limit indemnification to your acts and omissions.
Scan for unilateral rights: can they change terms, raise prices, or assign the contract without your consent? Require mutual consent for changes.
Scan for termination traps: what happens on termination? Is there a penalty? Do you retain your data and IP? Is there a transition period?

description: Negotiate salary using the same principles as any negotiation but applied to the specific dynamics of employment. Know your market value, understand the employer's constraints, negotiate the full package (not just base), and get the offer before discussing numbers.

steps.description: Research your market value before any salary discussion. Your market value is what other employers would pay for your skills, not what you currently earn.

outputs.name: market-range
outputs.desc: The salary range for this role in this market: 25th percentile, median, 75th percentile, and 90th percentile, with sources

outputs.name: positioning-rationale
outputs.desc: Where you fall in the range based on your specific qualifications, with the evidence

process: Research salary data from multiple sources: industry surveys, job postings with salary ranges, recruiter conversations, peer data, and public salary databases.
Identify the range for your specific role, location, industry, and company size. National averages are too broad.
Position yourself in the range based on your differentiators: years of experience, specialized skills, certifications, track record, and the specific value you bring.
Your current salary is irrelevant to your market value. Do not anchor to what you earn now.

steps.description: Negotiate the full compensation package, not just the base salary. Base salary is one component. Equity, bonus, benefits, flexibility, title, and development budget can add significant value.

outputs.name: package-priorities
outputs.desc: All compensation components ranked by value to you: base, equity, bonus, signing bonus, PTO, remote flexibility, title, learning budget, severance

outputs.name: negotiation-script
outputs.desc: The specific language for the salary discussion: how to deflect early salary questions, how to present your ask, and how to counter their offer

process: List every compensation component: base salary, equity (options or RSUs), annual bonus, signing bonus, PTO/vacation, remote work flexibility, title, learning/development budget, relocation, severance terms.
Rank these by personal value: some people value equity higher, others value flexibility. Know your priorities before the conversation.
If base salary is capped (budget constraints), negotiate other components: more equity, a signing bonus, additional PTO, or a guaranteed review at 6 months.

Prepare responses for salary questions: if asked for salary expectations before receiving an offer, defer ('I would like to understand the full role before discussing compensation' or 'What is the range budgeted for this role?').

steps.description: Handle the offer: never accept immediately, counter with justification, and get the final terms in writing.

outputs.name: response-plan
outputs.desc: Step-by-step: express enthusiasm, ask for time, evaluate against market data, prepare counter, deliver counter with justification

outputs.name: counter-offer-template
outputs.desc: The specific counter-offer with each component, the ask, and the justification for each adjustment

process: Step 1: Express genuine enthusiasm for the role. This is not fake. You want the offer to improve, not to disappear.
Step 2: Ask for time to evaluate ('I am excited about this opportunity. Could I have until [date] to review the full offer?'). Never counter on the spot.
Step 3: Evaluate the offer against your market research and priorities. Identify the gaps: where is the offer below market or below your target?

Step 4: Counter with justification: 'Based on [market data/my experience/the role scope], I was expecting [target] for [component]. Is there flexibility here?' Counter on the most important components first.

description: Coordinate negotiations with more than two parties. Multi-party negotiations are not bilateral negotiations repeated. Coalitions form, information asymmetries multiply, and the agreement must satisfy enough parties to hold. Map the parties, identify natural coalitions, and build winning coalitions before the table convenes.

steps.description: Map every party: their interests, their power, their alternatives, and their relationships to other parties.

outputs.name: party-profiles
outputs.desc: For each party: their key interests, their power (veto, resources, information, alternatives), and their likely priorities

outputs.name: relationship-map
outputs.desc: How each party relates to the others: allies, opponents, neutral, dependent, or competitive

process: For each party, assess: what do they want? Why? What is their BATNA? What power do they hold (can they veto? control resources? hold information others need?)?
Map relationships: which parties are natural allies (shared interests)? Which are natural opponents (conflicting interests)? Which are swing parties (could go either way)?
Identify information asymmetries: who knows what? Information advantages create negotiating power.
Assess decision rules: does the agreement require unanimity, majority, or the consent of specific parties (veto holders)?

steps.description: Build a winning coalition: a group of parties whose combined support is sufficient for agreement. Approach allies first, then swing parties.

outputs.name: coalition-strategy
outputs.desc: The target coalition: which parties to approach, in what order, with what proposals

outputs.name: sequencing-plan
outputs.desc: The order of bilateral conversations before the full group convenes: build agreements with allies first, then approach swing parties with momentum

process: Identify the minimum winning coalition: the fewest parties whose agreement is sufficient for the deal to proceed.
Start with natural allies: approach parties with shared interests first. Build preliminary agreement on the issues where you align.
Approach swing parties with a coalition: 'Parties A, B, and I have agreed on this framework. We would like your input on...' Momentum creates pressure to join rather than block.
Isolate opponents: if a party's interests are fundamentally opposed, do not try to convert them first. Build a coalition around them and offer them a face-saving concession last.

steps.description: Design the agreement structure for multi-party deals. The agreement must be stable: no subset of parties should prefer to break away and form their own deal.

outputs.name: agreement-framework
outputs.desc: The deal structure: who gets what on each issue, how disputes are resolved, and how the agreement adapts to changing circumstances

outputs.name: stability-test
outputs.desc: For each subset of parties: would they prefer to break away? If yes, the agreement is unstable and must be adjusted.

process: Design the agreement so that each party gets more from the deal than from their BATNA. If any party is worse off in the deal than out of it, they will eventually defect.
Test for coalition stability: could any two or three parties form a side deal that is better for them? If yes, the agreement is unstable. Adjust the terms to remove the incentive for defection.
Include dispute resolution: multi-party agreements will face disagreements during implementation. Specify the process: who decides, how, and what happens if someone breaches.
Include adaptation mechanisms: markets and circumstances change. The agreement should specify how terms can be renegotiated without requiring the full multi-party process again.

description: Design your concession strategy: what to give, when to give it, how to give it, and what to get in return. Concessions are signals. Giving too much too fast signals desperation. Giving nothing signals inflexibility. The right pattern of concessions communicates reasonableness while protecting your position.

steps.description: Inventory everything you can concede, ranked by cost to you and value to them.

outputs.name: concession-inventory
outputs.desc: Every possible concession, with: cost to you (low/medium/high), estimated value to them (low/medium/high), and conditions (what you would want in return)

outputs.name: high-value-low-cost-concessions
outputs.desc: Concessions that cost you little but are valued highly by the other party: these are your trading chips

process: List everything you could give: price adjustments, timeline changes, scope additions, flexibility, guarantees, options, information, introductions, references.
For each, assess the cost to you: does this actually cost you something material, or is it low-cost to provide?
For each, estimate the value to them: is this something they care about deeply, or is it minor to them?
The best concessions are low-cost to you and high-value to them. These give you maximum leverage at minimum cost.

steps.description: Design the concession pattern: how to sequence and size concessions to signal reasonableness while protecting your position.

outputs.name: concession-sequence
outputs.desc: The planned order and size of concessions: start large, then smaller, then smaller, signaling approach to your limit

outputs.name: reciprocity-requirements
outputs.desc: What you require in return for each concession: never concede without receiving

process: First concession: the largest. It signals goodwill and willingness to negotiate. But it must come with a request: 'I can move to X on this issue. In return, I need Y on that issue.'
Subsequent concessions: each one smaller than the previous. The decreasing size signals that you are approaching your limit. If your first move was 20%, the second should be 10%, the third 5%.
Never make a concession without getting one in return. If they ask for something, respond with: 'I can consider that. What can you offer on [issue]?'
Label your concessions: 'This is a significant move for me because [reason].' Unlabeled concessions are taken for granted. Labeled concessions build reciprocity pressure.

steps.description: Handle deadline pressure and last-minute demands. Deadlines create urgency that leads to bad concessions. Separate real deadlines from manufactured pressure.

outputs.name: deadline-assessment
outputs.desc: For each deadline: is it real (external constraint) or manufactured (pressure tactic)? What happens if the deadline passes?

outputs.name: pressure-response-plan
outputs.desc: How to respond to last-minute demands, take-it-or-leave-it offers, and artificial urgency without making panic concessions

process: When a deadline is imposed, ask: what happens if we miss it? If the answer is 'nothing material,' the deadline is manufactured. If there are real consequences (regulatory filing, budget cycle, project start), it is real.
Real deadlines: work backward from the deadline. Know your minimum acceptable deal and your walk-away point before the deadline pressure intensifies.
Manufactured deadlines: name the tactic. 'I understand the urgency, but I want to make sure we reach the right agreement, not just a fast one. Can we extend to [date]?'
Last-minute demands (adding a new issue at the final stage): never accept without trading. 'I was not expecting this issue. I need to reassess the entire package if we are adding new terms.'
